sentences.text: The known fossil consists of a single, robust vertebra measuring 539 mm across, which features large air-filled cavities called pleurocoels to keep the bone light.
This vertebra displays a unique trait where the neural spines are divided into a U-shaped cleft, a feature also seen in its relative Mamenchisaurus.
Although the specimen is nearly complete, a portion of the right diapophysis was damaged and later repaired with plaster.
The name Hudiesaurus translates to "butterfly lizard," a reference to the split neural spines of the holotype vertebra.
Some estimates suggest this dinosaur reached a massive length of 32 meters and a weight of 55 tonnes.
The genus was formally described by Chinese paleontologist Dong Zhiming in 1997.
Fossils were first unearthed in 1993 by the Sino-Japanese Silk Road Dinosaur Expedition near Qiketai in the Turpan Basin.
The initial find included a presacral vertebra, an incomplete right forelimb, and four teeth located in quarries roughly one kilometer apart.
As a member of the mamenchisaurid family, Hudiesaurus was likely a four-legged herbivore that fed on vegetation at low to medium heights.
Paleontologists Mark Hallet and Matt Wedel theorized that the split neural spines allowed the animal to browse at high elevations.
However, other studies propose that these spines indicate a horizontal neck posture rather than the ability to reach high branches.
Researchers Rubén Molina-Pérez and Asier Larremendi estimated the animal at 30.5 meters long and 44 tonnes if the vertebra is dorsal, but 32 meters and 55 tonnes if it is cervical.
Hudiesaurus belongs to the class Saurischia and is classified within the family Mamenchisauridae.
Its size was comparable to other mamenchisaurids such as Xinjiangtitan, which measured 30 to 32 meters, and Mamenchisaurus sinocanodorum at 26 meters.
Some researchers, including Upchurch, have argued that Hudiesaurus should be classified as an indeterminate eusauropod instead of a specific mamenchisaurid.
This dinosaur lived during the Late Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages, approximately 154 to 143 million years ago, or more precisely between 152.21 and 143.1 million years ago.
Fossils are found in the lower section of the Kalaza Formation within the Turpan and Junggar Basins in China, preserved in thick red sandstones and mudstones.
The environment consisted of terrestrial or river-deposited sediments forming alluvial deltas in a warm, seasonally dry climate before conditions became more arid.
There is a debate regarding the position of the holotype vertebra, with initial identification as a dorsal vertebra later challenged by analysis suggesting it is a cervical vertebra.
In 2004, Paul Upchurch and colleagues criticized the assignment of a forelimb and teeth to Hudiesaurus due to insufficient evidence.
